title: MM-SCALE: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Moral Judgment in Vision-Language Models
claim: A benchmark pairs each input with multiple annotated scenarios and defines several complementary tasks that jointly test evidence-grounded judgment.
layout: 2 sections: data example on top, three task flow panels below
description: The figure has two parts. Part A, "MM-SCALE data example", shows one photo of a man looking overheated on a park bench with an older stranger beside him. Lines branch from the photo to three color-coded scenario rows: green S1 (offering water), orange S2 (accepting an opened bottle from a stranger), and red S3 (pressuring someone to drink). Each row has a rating (4.6/5, 3.0/5, 1.3/5) and a modality-grounding label (image, both, text). Part B shows three dotted-border task panels. Each is a left-to-right flow: an Input box, a robot icon, an Output box, and a blue Ground Truth box, with a dotted connector to a Goal caption. Task 3 adds a yellow Evidence Verifier box. Colored headers label Input, Output and Ground Truth.
caption: Overview of MM-SCALE. (A) Each image context is paired with multiple action scenarios. Each image–scenario pair has a human mean moral acceptability rating and a human modality-grounding label (whether the score depends on text, image, or both). (B) Three benchmark tasks. Task 1 evaluates scalar moral acceptability rating, which is compared to the mean human rating. Task 2 evaluates within-image moral ordering. Task 3 evaluates evidence-dependent rationale grounding: a verifier predicts which evidence source the rationale makes necessary for the verdict, and this predicted evidence label is compared with the human modality-grounding label.
abstract: Vision-Language Models increasingly make socially consequential judgments from image-text inputs, yet current evaluations often stop at verdict-level accuracy: whether the final label is human-aligned, not whether it follows from the correct evidence. We introduce MM-SCALE (Multimodal Moral SCALE), a benchmark for evidence-grounded moral judgment built around a design choice: each image is paired with multiple action scenarios, so models must compare how different actions interact with the same visual context rather than score images in isolation. MM-SCALE contains 8,444 image contexts and 21,977 action scenarios, each annotated with a 5-point moral acceptability rating and a modality-grounding label indicating whether the human judgment relied on text, image, or both. Three tasks evaluate whether models (i) assign calibrated scalar moral scores, (ii) preserve human orderings within a shared visual context, and (iii) ground rationales in the evidence source humans found critical to judgment. Across models, aggregate metrics overstate alignment: NDCG@5 remains high across models, while within-image pairwise accuracy remains only 0.53-0.62 even on scenario pairs whose human mean ratings differ by at least one point. CoT has inconsistent effects on calibration and does not reliably improve within-image ordering. Evidence grounding evaluations further show that models often describe visual context without making it critical for the verdict. These results reveal an evidence-grounding failure in current VLMs and position MM-SCALE as an evaluation testbed for moral judgment under shared image contexts. This dataset includes potentially harmful and sensitive visual content. Images are intended solely for evaluation.
